A boilermaker before West Point, this U.S. general graduated in 1915 alongside Dwight Eisenhower in "the class the stars fell on" and later became the first chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff — who is he?
Omar Bradley: United States Army general (1893–1981)

At 93, this Cameroonian head of state is the world's oldest sitting president and the second-longest-ruling leader in Africa, having taken power in 1982 after his predecessor's surprise resignation — who is he?
Paul Biya: President of Cameroon since 1982.

After leaving his party in 2021, this Dutch politician founded a new party called New Social Contract, which won 20 seats in the 2023 election, and helped expose the childcare benefits scandal — who is he?
Alfred, Duke of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha
Commander of Iran's Quds Force from 1998 until his assassination by the United States in 2020, he was called the single most powerful operative in the Middle East — who was he?

Modeled on a notorious wave of Revolutionary France violence, this campaign of political repression and mass executions was carried out by the Bolshevik secret police during the Russian Civil War — what is it called?
Red Terror: Bolshevik campaign of political repression and executions (1918–1922)
The first Philippine president from Mindanao and the oldest to take office at 71, this former Davao City mayor led the country from 2016 — who is it?
Rodrigo Duterte: President of the Philippines from 2016 to 2022.
The oldest daughter of her husband's own uncle, this woman was the wife of former Iraqi president Saddam Hussein and mother to sons Uday and Qusay — who is she?
Sajida Talfah: First wife of Saddam Hussein.

Proclaimed in 1852 when a president crowned himself Napoleon III, this 18-year regime built out a national railway network even as historians later judged its foreign policy a failure — what was this government called?
Second French Empire: France under Napoleon III (1852–1870)
Currently Japan's Minister of Defense, this LDP lawmaker representing Kanagawa is the son of a former prime minister and once worked as his father's political secretary — who is he?
Married to the youngest sibling of King Charles III since 1999, this member of the British royal family previously worked in public relations before her wedding at Windsor Castle — who is she?
Sophie, Duchess of Edinburgh: Member of the British royal family (born 1965)

This Prince of Kiev, who ruled from 945 to 972, conquered rival Slavic tribes and helped bring down both Khazaria and the First Bulgarian Empire, carving out the largest state in Europe at the time — who was he?
Sviatoslav I: Prince of Kiev from 945 to 972. Following the death of his father Igor in 945, Sviatoslav's mother Olga reigned as regent in Kiev until 962.
Central to Judaism and recounted every Passover, this founding narrative describes the Israelites' escape from Egyptian bondage through a parting of the Red Sea under Moses — what is it?
The Exodus: Founding myth of the Jewish people.

Regarded as the founding father of his nation, this philosopher-turned-statesman served as its first president from 1918 to 1935 after campaigning across Europe for independence during World War I — who is he?
Tomáš Masaryk: Founding father of Czechoslovakia (1850–1937)

Going by VGE, this finance-minister-turned-president eked out a 1974 win over François Mitterrand with 50.8% of the vote, then liberalized French law on divorce, contraception, and abortion — who was he?
Valéry Giscard d'Estaing: President of France from 1974 to 1981.
Hitler called him one of his best field commanders and kept dispatching him to salvage collapsing fronts — which hard-driving German field marshal became famous as a master of defensive warfare?
Nicknamed the "Sailor King" for his Royal Navy youth, he was the last king of the House of Hanover and once spent two decades living with the actress Dorothea Jordan — who was he?
William IV: King of the United Kingdom from 1830 to 1837.
The first woman to hold her position, this French politician has led the National Assembly since June 2022 and briefly served as Minister of the Overseas before that — who is she?
Grand Duchess Maria Vladimirovna of Russia
His famous epithet is actually a pun on his name — "noble" plus "counsel" — and this King of the English took the throne after his half-brother Edward the Martyr was assassinated. Who was he?
Æthelred the Unready: King of England (r. 978–1013; 1014–1016)
Which of these four was born earliest?
Henrietta Swan Leavitt (born 1868) is the earliest of the four. Henrietta Swan Leavitt (July 4, 1868 – December 12, 1921) was an American astronomer.
Which of these people was born first?
Zhuge Liang (born 181) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four dates back furthest?
Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four began earliest?
Pascal (programming language) (founded 1970) is the earliest of the four. It is named after French mathematician, philosopher and physicist Blaise Pascal.
Pick the astronomer from these four.
Galileo Galilei is an astronomer. Galileo has been called the father of observational astronomy, modern-era classical physics, the scientific method, and modern science.
Which one below is best known as a mathematician?
Blaise Pascal is a mathematician. Blaise Pascal (19 June 1623 – 19 August 1662) was a French mathematician, physicist, inventor, philosopher, and Catholic writer.
What is the atomic number of Unbinilium?
Unbinilium, also known as eka-radium or element 120, is a hypothetical chemical element; it has symbol Ubn and atomic number 120.
What is the atomic number of Arsenic?
Arsenic is a chemical element; it has the symbol As and atomic number 33.
In what year was Ted Kaczynski born?
Ted Kaczynski: The FBI used the case identifier UNABOM (University and Airline Bombing) before his identity was known, resulting in the media naming him the "Unabomber".
In what year was Steve Wozniak born?
Steve Wozniak: In 1976, he co-founded Apple Computer (now Apple Inc.) with his early business partner Steve Jobs.
In what year was Dmitri Mendeleev born?
Dmitri Mendeleev: The synthetic element mendelevium is named in his honor.
In what year did Ptolemy die?
Ptolemy: The first was his astronomical treatise now known as the Almagest, originally entitled Mathēmatikḗ Syntaxis (Μαθηματικὴ Σύνταξις, 'Mathematical Treatise').
In what year did Al-Khwarizmi die?
Al-Khwarizmi: Few biographical details are known about al-Khwarizmi's life.
In what year was Nitrogen discovered?
Nitrogen is a chemical element; it has symbol N and atomic number 7.
Which company manufactures Lockheed F-117 Nighthawk?
Lockheed F-117 Nighthawk: Skunk Works. It was the first operational aircraft to be designed with stealth technology.
In which country is Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-21 based?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-21: Soviet Union. Approximately 60 countries across four continents have flown the MiG-21, and it still serves many nations seven decades after its maiden flight.
Who is credited with discovering Triangulum Australe?
Triangulum Australe: Américo Vespucio. Triangulum Australe is a small constellation in the far Southern Celestial Hemisphere.
Who is credited with discovering Ichthyosaurus?
Ichthyosaurus: Mary Anning. It is among the best known ichthyosaur genera, as it is the type genus of the order Ichthyosauria.
Who is credited with discovering Theobroma cacao?
Theobroma cacao: Christopher Columbus. Theobroma cacao (cacao tree or cocoa tree) is a small (6–12 m (20–39 ft) tall) evergreen tree in the Malvaceae family.
Who is credited with discovering Krypton?
Krypton: William Ramsay. Krypton (from Ancient Greek: κρυπτός, romanized: kryptos 'the hidden one') is a chemical element; it has symbol Kr and atomic number 36.

A German-born theoretical physicist best known for developing the theory of relativity, his mass–energy formula E=mc2 comes from special relativity and has been called "the world's most famous equation." Born in 1879, who won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics?
Albert Einstein (14 March 1879 - 18 April 1955) was a German-born theoretical physicist best known for developing the known theory of relativity.
Famed for foundational work in number theory and algebraic geometry, this French mathematician was also a principal founder of the secretive Bourbaki group — who was he?
André Weil (6 May 1906 - 6 August 1998) was a French mathematician, known for his foundational work in number theory and algebraic geometry.
This mid-sized zodiac constellation, sitting between Pisces and Taurus, has represented a ram since late Babylonian times — though its stars once formed a farmhand. Which one is it?
Aries (constellation) is one of the constellations of the zodiac. It is located in the Northern celestial hemisphere between Pisces to the west and Taurus to the east.

Developed in Great Britain around the 1830s from breeds like the Talbot Hound, this scent hound — smaller than the similar-looking foxhound — was originally bred to hunt rabbits and hares — name the breed?
Beagle is a British breed of scent hound, similar in appearance to the much larger foxhound.
Native to cool parts of Europe and Asia, this deciduous shrub produces small, glossy black berries especially rich in vitamin C and vulnerable to cold snaps during spring flowering — name the fruit?
Blackcurrant (Ribes nigrum), black currant or cassis is a deciduous shrub in the family Grossulariaceae grown for its edible berries.

Forced to flee Italy in 1938 under the racial laws, this experimental physicist had earlier invented an improved coincidence circuit and traveled to Eritrea to show cosmic rays arrived more strongly from the West than the East — who was he?
Bruno Rossi (13 April 1905 - 21 November 1993) was an Italian-American experimental physicist.
A child prodigy who became director of the Göttingen Observatory, this German polymath left his mark on number theory, algebra, geometry, statistics, and probability alike — who is he?
Carl Friedrich Gauss (30 April 1777 - 23 February 1855) was a German mathematician, astronomer, geodesist, and physicist, who contributed to many fields in mathematics and science.
Atomic number 17, this strongly oxidising yellow-green gas sits between fluorine and bromine on the periodic table — what element is it?
Chlorine is a chemical element; it has symbol Cl and atomic number 17.
This bird group's rock-dove species gave rise to most domesticated pigeon breeds, including racing and fantail pigeons, and was later introduced to the Americas — which classification is it?
Columba (genus) comprises a genus of medium to large pigeons.
This actor known for eccentric roles broke out playing a teenager's awkward father in a 1985 time-travel classic. Who is he?
Crow is a bird of the genus Corvus, or more broadly, a synonym for all of Corvus.
Its genus name translates to 'two-crested lizard,' honoring the twin head-crests found on fossils unearthed in Arizona in the 1940s — which Early Jurassic predator is this?
Dilophosaurus (dy-, -foh-) is a genus of theropod dinosaurs that lived in what is now North America during the Early Jurassic, about 186 million years ago.
Element 99 was first found in the radioactive debris of the very first hydrogen bomb blast in 1952 — which synthetic actinide is it?
Einsteinium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Es and atomic number 99 and is a member of the actinide series and the seventh transuranium element.
Also called grain alcohol, this volatile compound with the formula C2H5OH is the active ingredient in every alcoholic beverage — what is it?
Ethanol (also called ethyl alcohol, grain alcohol, drinking alcohol, or simply alcohol) is an organic compound with the chemical formula CH3CH2OH.
Found on sperm cells, fungal spores and countless microbes, this tail-like structure provides motility and even senses moisture in some swarming bacteria — what is it?

Flagellum (pl.: flagella) (Latin for 'whip' or 'scourge') is a hair-like appendage that protrudes from certain plant and animal sperm cells, from fungal spores (zoospores), and from a wide range of microorganisms to provide motility.
Native to Pacific coastal waters from Alaska to Baja California, this giant burrowing clam can grow a siphon over three feet long and live for more than a century — which creature?
Geoduck (Panopea generosa) is a species of very large saltwater clam in the family Hiatellidae.
One of only two wild camelid species native to South America, this llama relative lives at lower elevations than its cousin, the vicuña — what is it called?
Guanaco (gwah-; Lama guanicoe) is a camelid native to South America, closely related to the domesticated llama.
Never approved by any drug regulator, this THC-like compound made by hydrogenating cannabis isomers has been sold in head-shop vaporizers since the early 2020s — what is it?
Hexahydrocannabinol (HHC) is a phytocannabinoid that has been reported as a minor component of Cannabis oleoresin.
About the size of an almond in humans, this small brain region links the nervous system to the endocrine system via the pituitary gland — what is it?
Hypothalamus (pl.: hypothalami; from Ancient Greek (hup) 'under' and (thlamos) 'chamber') is a small part of the vertebrate brain that contains a number of nuclei with a variety of functions.
Serving as president of the European Commission from 1985 to 1995, this French politician played a central role in creating the European single market and laying groundwork for the euro — who is he?
Jacques Delors (20 July 1925 - 27 December 2023) was a French politician who served as president of the European Commission from 1985 to 1995.

This 20th-century Peruvian writer of mestizo descent composed novels, poems, and stories in both Spanish and Quechua, and even coined a new literary idiom to render Indigenous perspective more authentically — who is he?
José María Arguedas (Spanish) was a Peruvian novelist, poet, and anthropologist.
This inflammation of the voice box causes symptoms ranging from a hoarse voice to complete voice loss, usually clearing up within two weeks. Name the condition?
Laryngitis is inflammation of the larynx (voice box). The primary symptom is loss of some vocal function, ranging from hoarse voice to no voice at all.
Only about 35 atoms of this synthetic element (symbol Lv, number 116) had ever been made as of 2020 — named for a California national laboratory. Which element is it?
Livermorium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Lv and atomic number 116.
Sometimes nicknamed 'sea cows,' these large, fully aquatic herbivorous marine mammals can grow up to 13 feet long and include Amazonian, West Indian, and West African species — what are they called?
Manatee (family Trichechidae, genus Trichechus) are large, fully aquatic, mostly herbivorous marine mammals sometimes known as sea cows.
Together with the Focke-Wulf Fw 190, this monoplane fighter formed the backbone of the Luftwaffe's fighter force throughout the Second World War. What aircraft is it?
Messerschmitt Bf 109 is a monoplane fighter aircraft that was designed and initially produced by the German aircraft manufacturer Bayerische Flugzeugwerke (BFW).
This unique group of mammals is the only one whose members lay eggs rather than bear live young, comprising the platypus and four echidna species — what group is it?
Monotreme are mammals of the order Monotremata.

Encompassing several types of kidney inflammation affecting the glomeruli, tubules, or nearby interstitial tissue, this general medical term falls under the broader category of nephropathy — what's the condition?
Nephritis is inflammation of the kidneys and may involve the glomeruli, tubules, or interstitial tissue surrounding the glomeruli and tubules.
This English physicist identified electromagnetic radiation independently of Hertz, and named his improved early radio receiver the 'coherer' — whose key 'syntonic' tuning patents helped birth radio?
Oliver Lodge (12 June 1851 - 22 August 1940) was an English physicist and electrical engineer whose investigations into electromagnetic radiation (EMR) contributed to the development of radio.

Closely related to carrot and parsley, this pale, long-tapered root vegetable grows sweeter in flavor after winter frosts and produces yellow flowers if left unharvested into its second season — name the vegetable?
Parsnip (Pastinaca sativa) is a root vegetable closely related to carrot and parsley, all belonging to the flowering plant family Apiaceae.
Made in the body from the amino acid L-phenylalanine, this natural stimulant also turns up in fermented chocolate and inhibits a transporter called VMAT2 — what is it?
Phenethylamine (PEA) is an organic compound, natural monoamine alkaloid, and trace amine, which acts as a central nervous system stimulant in humans.
It looks like a single point of light, but this brightest star of Ursa Minor is actually a triple star system parked near the north celestial pole — what is it?
Polaris is a yellow supergiant star in the northern circumpolar constellation of Ursa Minor.

This sympathomimetic medication is best known as a nasal decongestant, though at higher doses it can act as a stimulant and appetite suppressant, making it a common drug of abuse — what's the compound called?
Pseudoephedrine is a sympathomimetic medication which is used as a nasal decongestant to treat nasal congestion.
With roughly 12,000 living species split across four classic orders — including the single-species tuatara branch — what ectothermic class is this?
Reptile are tetrapod vertebrate animals with an ectothermic metabolism and amniotic development.

Originally conceived in the 1960s as a jet trainer before evolving into a supersonic strike aircraft, this joint British-French warplane — retired by both original operators — remains in service only with the Indian Air Force. Name it?
SEPECAT Jaguar is a British-French supersonic jet attack aircraft originally used by the British Royal Air Force and the French Air Force in the close air support and nuclear strike role.
Born into a Russian-Jewish family in Moscow and brought to the US at age six, which co-founder of Google served as president of Alphabet until 2019?
Sergey Brin (born August 21, 1973) is an American computer scientist and businessman who co-founded Google with Larry Page.
Made simply from ice mixed with fruit juice or purée, plus the occasional splash of wine or honey, this dairy-free frozen treat goes by what name?
Sorbet is a frozen dessert made using ice combined with fruit juice, fruit pure, or other ingredients, such as wine, liqueur, or honey.
This artificial sweetener is produced by chlorinating ordinary table sugar and is roughly 600 times sweeter than sucrose — three times sweeter even than aspartame — what's the sweetener called?

Sucralose is an artificial sweetener and sugar substitute. The commercial success of sucralose-based products stems from its favorable comparison to other low-calorie sweeteners in terms of taste, stability, and safety.
A colorless, water-miscible cyclic ether and a versatile solvent, this compound is mainly used as a precursor to polymers and is an isomer of butanone — what is it?
Tetrahydrofuran (THF), or oxolane, is an organic compound with the formula (CH2)4O.
When water loss to the air outpaces uptake by the roots, plants shut tiny leaf pores to conserve moisture, slowing this evaporative water-movement process — what's it called?
Transpiration is the process of water movement through a plant and its evaporation from aerial parts, such as leaves, stems and flowers.
This British-American structural biologist shared the 2009 Nobel in Chemistry for revealing the ribosome's structure and later led the Royal Society as president — who is he?
Venki Ramakrishnan (born 1952) is a British-American structural biologist.
This biological process unfolds in predictable phases — hemostasis, inflammation, cell proliferation, and tissue remodeling — to replace damaged skin after the barrier is broken. What is it?
Wound healing refers to a living organism's replacement of destroyed or damaged tissue by newly produced tissue.
This mucolytic drug is the go-to antidote for acetaminophen overdose, working by boosting glutathione to neutralize the drug's toxic byproducts — what is it?
Acetylcysteine: Medication used to treat overdose of paracetamol.
Twice President of the Swiss Confederation, this Social Democratic politician left the Federal Council in 2023 to become Secretary General of the Council of Europe — who is he?
Alain Berset: Swiss Federal Councillor from 2012 to 2023.

Native to South Africa's Western Cape, this flowering bulb genus lends its common name to popular winter houseplants that actually belong to a different genus, Hippeastrum — which bulb, also called the naked lady or Jersey lily?
Amaryllis: Genus of plants. Amaryllis is the only genus in the subtribe Amaryllidinae (tribe Amaryllideae).
Named by paleontologist Barnum Brown in 1908, this armored dinosaur is considered the archetypal member of its group despite no complete skeleton ever being found — which genus?
Ankylosaurus: Ankylosaurid dinosaur genus from the Late Cretaceous Period.
Also called gobō, this Eurasian plant is cultivated in Japan for its edible root but has become an invasive weed of high-nitrogen soils elsewhere — which species?
Arctium lappa: Species of flowering plant. It has become an invasive weed of high-nitrogen soils in North America, Australia, and other regions, but is cultivated for its vegetable root.
This British mathematician and logician coined the phrase 'mathematical induction' and gave his name to a pair of laws relating conjunction, disjunction, and negation. Who was he?
Augustus De Morgan: British mathematician and logician (1806–1871)
In continuous production since 1974 — the longest run of any civilian turboprop plane in its class — this twin-engine model also serves in medevac and flight-inspection roles — what is it?
Beechcraft Super King Air: Light twin-turboprop transport aircraft family.
Recognizable by its angled wings and forked tail, this scavenging bird of prey is thought to be the world's most abundant raptor, with a global population topping six million — which bird?
Black kite: Species of bird. The black kite or fire kite (Milvus migrans) is a medium-sized bird of prey in the family Accipitridae, which also includes many other diurnal raptors.
Named for the 18th-century French explorer who documented it on one of his expeditions, this thorny ornamental vine produces colorful bracts around three small waxy flowers — which plant is it?
First proposed after the 1964 murder of Kitty Genovese, this psychological theory says people are less likely to help a victim when others are present — what's it called?
Bystander effect: Social psychological theory. Recent research has focused on "real world" events captured on security cameras, and the coherency and robustness of the effect has come under question.

This polyatomic ion, CO3 with a 2- charge, is dissolved into water under pressure to make it fizzy, and also makes up much of the sedimentary rock in the Earth's crust — what's the ion (and salt) called?
Carbonate: Salt or ester of carbonic acid.
Discovered in 1945 and first sold in 1964, this class of beta-lactam antibiotics was originally pulled from a fungus once known as Cephalosporium — what's the family called?
Made in the skin after sun exposure and also known as vitamin D3, this compound is converted by the liver and kidneys into forms that help the body absorb calcium. What is it?

Cholecalciferol: Vitamin D3, a chemical compound. Cholecalciferol, also known as vitamin D3, colecalciferol or calciol, is a skin-made vitamin D that is found in certain foods and used as a dietary supplement.
First described by Linnaeus in 1758 and introduced to North America to control aphids, this red beetle with seven black spots gets its genus name from the Latin word for 'scarlet' — which species?
Coccinella septempunctata: Species of beetle. It inhabits many regions with a temperate climate.
This mathematical framework assigns one or more numbers to each point in space so its exact position can be pinned down — the foundation of analytic geometry. What is it called?
Coordinate system: Method for specifying point positions.

First described by Linnaeus in 1767, this citrus-family plant native to the Indian subcontinent has aromatic leaves essential to South Asian cooking, especially in India and Sri Lanka — which species?

Curry tree: Species of flowering plant. It is native to the Indian subcontinent, southern China and mainland Southeast Asia, and it has been introduced to other parts of southeast Asia and to Australia.
Nicknamed the 'gympie-gympie' by Queensland's Gubbi Gubbi people, this Australian and Malaysian rainforest plant delivers an infamously painful, long-lasting sting. What species is it?
Dendrocnide moroides: Species of plant in the nettle family.
A Canadian optical physicist at Waterloo, she shared the 2018 Nobel in Physics for the practical implementation of chirped pulse amplification — who is she?
Donna Strickland: Canadian physicist, engineer, and Nobel laureate.
Credited as the first to create a transuranium element — neptunium — this Berkeley physicist shared the 1951 Nobel in Chemistry with Glenn Seaborg. Who was he?
Also called Human Factors Engineering, this discipline applies psychology and physiology to reduce errors and boost safety in system design — what field?
Ergonomics: Designing systems to suit their users.
One of only two living species in its genus, this rodent was such a prized delicacy to the ancient Romans that its common name literally advertises the fact. What animal is it?
European edible dormouse: Species of rodent.

Marked by widespread chronic pain plus fatigue and foggy thinking, this condition affects 2 to 4% of people, more often women, and was first recognised in the 1950s but only defined in 1990 — what is it?
Dubbed the "Flying Tailor," this inventor was so sure his wearable parachute would work that he leapt from the Eiffel Tower to test it himself — fatally. Who was he?
This scientific field measures Earth's precise shape, gravity, and orientation in space, underpinning satellite positioning systems and global mapping — which discipline?
Geodesy: Science of measuring the shape, orientation, and gravity of Earth.

Weighing up to 175 grams, this South American tarantula is the world's most massive spider — despite a name inspired by an 18th-century engraving of one eating a hummingbird, it rarely actually preys on birds. Which species?
Goliath birdeater: Species of tarantula from South America.

Caused by a retrovirus that attacks the immune system, this condition has no cure or vaccine — yet with antiretroviral treatment a person can now expect to live a normal life and die with the virus, not of it. What is it?
HIV/AIDS: Spectrum of conditions caused by HIV infection.
The only Saskatchewan-born Nobel laureate, this Canadian-born chemist won the 1983 prize for unraveling the mechanisms of electron-transfer reactions in metal complexes — who was he?

Galaxies recede from Earth at speeds proportional to their distance, a relationship credited to a 1929 paper — though the maths behind an expanding universe had already been derived in 1922 by Alexander Friedmann. What's this relationship called?
Hubble's law: Observation in physical cosmology.
This 14th-century Arab scholar wrote his most famous work, the Muqaddimah, in just six months and once met the conqueror Tamerlane — who is he?
Ibn Khaldun: Arab Islamic scholar, historian and philosopher (1332–1406)
This Russian physiologist won the 1904 Nobel Prize for his work on digestion, but is far better remembered for training dogs to salivate at a signal — who was he?
Once an assistant to astronomer Tycho Brahe and later imperial mathematician to Emperor Rudolf II, this polymath formulated the laws of planetary motion — who was he?
Johannes Kepler: German astronomer and mathematician (1571–1630)

A NASA mathematician and human computer, she calculated the orbital mechanics critical to America's first crewed spaceflights and was among the first African-American women to work as a NASA scientist — who was she?
Commonly called the voice box, which organ in the upper neck houses the vocal cords and protects the windpipe from food entering it?
Larynx: Voice box, an organ in the neck of amphibians, reptiles, and mammals.
The only person ever to win two unshared Nobel Prizes, this American chemist earned one for his work on the chemical bond and another for peace activism — who is he?
Linus Pauling: American scientist and activist (1901–1994)
This American experimental physicist won the 1968 Nobel Prize for discovering resonance states using the hydrogen bubble chamber — who was he?
Luis Walter Alvarez: American physicist, inventor and professor (1911–1988)

Often called the mirror image of depression, this psychiatric state brings racing thoughts, pressured speech, boundless energy, and a shrinking need for sleep — what is this elevated mood syndrome called?
Mania: State of abnormally elevated or irritable mood, arousal, and/or energy levels.
Developing from pigment-producing skin cells and most common on the legs in women and the back in men, about 30% of cases of this cancer arise from existing moles — what is it?
Melanoma: Skin cancer originating in melanocytes.
What is this — “Antiprogestogen and antiglucocorticoid drug”?
Mifepristone: Antiprogestogen and antiglucocorticoid drug. It is also used on its own to treat Cushing's syndrome or in low doses as an emergency contraceptive.
Native to tropical Central and South America, this genus of 59 flowering plant species belongs to the arum family — which genus?
Nicknamed the 'brain-eating amoeba,' this free-living microorganism lurks in warm freshwater lakes, hot springs, and poorly chlorinated pools — what is it?
A colorless gas with the formula NO, this free radical carries an unpaired electron and can be brewed by lightning in a thunderstorm. What molecule is it?
Nitric oxide: Colorless gas with the formula NO. Nitric oxide (nitrogen oxide, nitrogen mono-oxide, or nitrogen monoxide) is a colorless gas with the formula NO.
A Boston physician, medical reformer, and 'fireside' poet, this polymath delighted readers with his 'Breakfast-Table' series begun in 1858. Who was he?
Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.: American poet, essayist, physician (1809–1894)
With long dense grey fur and rounded ears set oddly low on the sides of its head, this small wild cat — first described in 1776 near Lake Baikal — roams the cold steppes of Central Asia. What is it?
Pallas's cat: Species of small wild cat. Pallas's cat (Otocolobus manul), also called manul, is a small wild cat with long and dense light grey fur, and rounded ears set low on the sides of the head.
Derived from Greek words meaning 'healer of children,' this branch of medicine covers care from infancy through adolescence — what is it?
Pediatrics: Branch of medicine caring for children. Within the Commonwealth, pediatrics covers patients until the age of 18, except in India where the pediatric age is 12.

Nicknamed 'banana spiders' and 'armed spiders' for their aggressive posture, this genus found mainly in northern South America is better known by a name describing its roaming habits — what genus is this?
Home to cereal crops like wheat, rice, and maize as well as bamboo, this is the fifth-largest plant family on Earth — what is it called?
Poaceae: Family of flowering plants commonly known as grasses.
This beta blocker treats high blood pressure and performance anxiety alike, and can even shrink capillary hemangiomas in infants — what drug?
Propranolol: Beta blocker drug. It can be taken orally, rectally, or by intravenous injection.
First identified in the 1950s as a radio source, this extremely luminous galactic nucleus can outshine an entire galaxy like the Milky Way thousands of times over — what is it?
Quasar: Active galactic nucleus (AGN) containing a supermassive black hole.
Native to South and Southeast Asia, this non-venomous constrictor is the world's longest snake and has been spotted swimming far out at sea — what species is it?
Reticulated python: Species of snake. It is the world's longest snake, and the third heaviest after the green anaconda and Burmese python.

Sold under the brand name Crestor, this medication lowers cholesterol by inhibiting an enzyme in the liver called HMG-CoA reductase, and was the twelfth most commonly prescribed drug in the US in 2023. What is it?
Rosuvastatin: Statin medication. It is recommended to be used with dietary changes, exercise, and weight loss.
Also called a green onion, this mild Allium vegetable has a slender green stem but never develops a bulb like its garlic and leek relatives — what is it?
Scallion: Edible vegetable of various species in the genus Allium.
Nicknamed the 'Human Computer' for her lightning mental arithmetic, this Indian writer also authored one of the earliest studies of homosexuality in India, back in 1977 — who is she?
Shakuntala Devi: Indian writer and mental calculator (1929–2013)
Known as caustic soda or lye, this white ionic solid is so corrosive it breaks down fats and proteins at room temperature and eagerly drinks moisture from the air — what compound is it?
Sodium hydroxide: Caustic soda, with formula NaOH.
